title: Are Extended Warranties Ever Worth It?
summary: A Wirecutter podcast episode lays out the math, psychology and business behind why extended warranties are usually a losing bet for buyers.

assertions.quote: The likelihood that the products will fail during the extended warranty period is quite low. People overestimate the failure rate

verdicts.note: Cited by multiple personal-finance researchers and reporters as a documented cognitive bias driving warranty purchases.

Abito & Salant find consumers substantially overestimate failure probabilities -- e.g. a product with a true ~5% failure rate is perceived, on average, as having a ~13.5% failure rate -- and show this, not risk aversion, drives warranty demand.

assertions.quote: it's an inconvenience with most consumer products if they break or need to be repaired

verdicts.note: The core argument from insurance economics: insurance is most valuable against losses too large to absorb, which most consumer-product repairs are not.

Abito & Salant note TV-warranty buyers pay $90+ on average to insure against a loss of at most $400 with a 7% probability -- too small an expected loss to be the kind of catastrophic risk true insurance protects against -- and find consumer welfare is negative in the status quo market.

assertions.quote: people are more susceptible to offers to buy extended warranties after they've decided to buy the product

verdicts.note: Supported by at least one cited behavioral study, though not universally replicated.

assertions.quote: the value that they offer to retailers... is increasing conversion rates

verdicts.note: Consistent with how embedded-insurance companies describe their own product to retailers.

assertions.quote: there is a mandatory 4-day cooling-off period

verdicts.note: Matches reported UK price-disclosure rules and Australia's mandatory cooling-off period.

assertions.quote: you should self-insure... put it into a savings account
it's going to be next-day service... he cannot afford to have the downtime

verdicts.note: A reasonable edge case, though faster repair could often be bought directly, such as paying for priority service, more cheaply than a warranty.
